Thanksgiving is a time to reflect upon the prior year, be thankful for what we have, gorge ourselves until we’re near bursting, and then settle into our favorite chairs and watch the first half of a TV show before the tryptophan kicks in. If you usually spend your post-meal time falling asleep to A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving, you won’t find it on the usual broadcast or cable channels–it’s exclusively on Apple TV.

Before you wave that turkey drumstick in the air and curse the state of television and all the darn streaming services you need subscriptions for—yes, I’m talking about you, Uncle Fred—you don’t need a subscription to Apple TV to watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving. Apple is making the show available to anyone for a limited time. If you are an Apple TV subscriber, however, you can watch it anytime.

How to watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving for free on Apple TV

On November 15 and 16, anyone with an Apple ID can watch A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving. If you own an Apple device, you have one, but if not, Apple IDs are free and you don’t need a credit card to sign up. Once you have signed up, you can watch in several ways:

  • Through the TV app on an iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
  • On smart TVs with the Apple TV app.
  • On the web at tv.apple.com.
  • On an Apple TV device.

As we noted when Apple did this same deal with It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, Apple has all the classic Peanuts specials for the holiday season that used to air over broadcast TV. Apple TV also has A Charlie Brown Christmas that will have its free airing on Dec. 12 and 13. Apple TV also has Happy New Year, Charlie Brown but it is not listed as free-to-view.

A few years ago, Apple acquired the rights to the Peanuts cartoon series that stars Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Linus, Lucy, and other memorable characters. Since then, Apple has aired new Peanuts shows such as The Snoopy Show and Snoopy in Space, and new movies, including Peanuts in Space: Secrets of Apollo 10, Lucy’s School, and It’s the Small Things, Charlie Brown.

The Apple TV subscription streaming service is $14.99/£9.99 per month. Apple TV is also included in the Apple One subscription bundles, which include other Apple services, such as Apple Music, Apple News+, and iCloud storage. Apple One bundles are priced between $21.95/£18.95 and $39.95/£36.95 per month.

For more information about Apple TV, read our Apple TV FAQ. We also have a detailed list of current Apple TV shows and upcoming shows.

Gaming subscription services are all the rage now, but Apple Arcade isn’t a little different from the likes of PlayStation Plus, EA Play, or Xbox Game Pass. If you’ve got questions about it, we’ve got plenty of answers.

Updated November 6, 2026: There are four new games on the service this month: Crossy Road Rush, Food Stylist — Design Game+, KAMI 2+, NBA 2K7 Arcade Edition.

What is Apple Arcade?

Apple Arcade is a gaming subscription service for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and AppleTV that features several hundred games. The games are a mix of genres and styles, and include original games you’ll only find on the service and others that can be found on the regular App Store or even other platforms. Live Rewind, one of the more compelling features demonstrated at the launch of the Apple Watch Series 12 back in September, has finally become available with the launch (in beta form) of watchOS 27.3 and iOS 27.3. I’ve spent several days testing Live Rewind, and can report that it’s a thoroughly impressive proof of concept. But there are flaws and limitations to be aware of, even if several of the latter are the result of good intentions.

Here are six takeaways from my extensive hands-on testing with Live Rewind on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Live Rewind is surprisingly accurate

I was skeptical, but Live Rewind does a surprisingly decent job of understanding and transcribing what it hears.

I started by playing YouTube videos of restaurant conversations for people learning English as a foreign language: slow, clear, with largely simple vocabulary. I sat close to the iPad playing the video. An easy task to begin with, and Live Rewind coped easily. The transcripts were virtually perfect, not to mention beautifully formatted with line breaks to denote separate short speeches.

I stepped up the difficulty by looking up some menus online (I selected this fancy restaurant) and acting the part of the waiter myself. I selected esoteric dishes I hadn’t heard of, spoke quickly and was careless with my enunciation, chucked in some ums and ers, varied volume and occasionally mumbled a little. And the feature produced a mostly accurate transcript that would have been extremely useful to a diner who had missed an option on the list.

This time the formatting was more of a challenge–Live Rewind couldn’t keep track of separate sentences, so the whole thing was jumbled together with a sometimes misleading number of commas–and occasionally I had to decipher a soundalike guess when the feature didn’t recognise a term. (“IV” instead of Ivy, “7 and Y” instead of the British rivers Severn and Wye, for example.) But the information was mostly there.

The most difficult task was when I used Live Rewind (after obtaining consent!) to recall snatches of random conversations with my family. This was more mixed. It caught the gist a lot of the time. But there were more soundalike guesses than before, and some sentences were missed entirely. This mostly related to distance, I think, and I’ll come back to that later.

So Live Recall is by no means perfect. But considering the difficulty of the task–handling variations in accent and diction, mumbling and muffled speech, irregular grammar, slang, in-jokes, proper nouns, brand names, technical or foreign terms–it does a very solid job. My verdict is that the accuracy is high enough to be useful as backup if you missed something, but not yet accurate enough to depend on as an alternative to paying attention.

David Price / Foundry

Live Rewind has a short memory

Like the proverbial goldfish, Live Rewind has a memory of 15 seconds. Which is shorter than you might think.

On one test I read out a list of just four main courses, but made sure to include the additional verbiage for each one, as I suspect many waiters in high-end establishments would be encouraged to do. Nothing extreme, just an extra sentence detailing ingredients and/or preparation. The result of this slight bulking out was that Live Rewind, despite being triggered the very moment I finished my list, missed a big chunk of it. The first main and half the second were lost to history.

Bear in mind, too, that while lists of specials in restaurants may frequently fit in the 15-second window (assuming the waiter refrains from prolixity), other scenarios may not work so well. Will the list of cocktails at a bar fit in 15 seconds, or the list of films at a cinema, or the list of changes your boss told you to make to a document? I have my doubts, although Siri Recap, if you use it, does not have a time limit and may be able to step in.

The short memory, it’s worth noting, applies whether or not Live Rewind is currently hearing anything. If you trigger the feature, it won’t rewind to the last 15 seconds of audio it heard; it will show you any speech it has heard in the past 15 seconds, ending when you double-press the Digital Crown. If you’ve been sitting in silence for at least 15 seconds, you’ll see the message “No voice detected.”

And even if you do manage to capture the transcript of some speech, Live Rewind will by default forget it the moment you tap the X button to close it. You need to explicitly save it to the Siri app if you want to keep the record. (You’ll save only the transcript, needless to say, not the audio from which it was created.)

This short memory is deliberate, by the way, as we’ll discover.

Live Rewind has a short range

My first impressions of the feature were not good. When I tried to use it on a conversation with my daughter, who was sitting perhaps 6 or 8 meters away and speaking unusually clearly, it produced a transcript of all my words and literally none of hers. But after more testing it became apparent that this was an issue of range, not accuracy. Live Rewind is good at picking up speech that’s close to you, and far less effective when someone is speaking even from the other side of the room.

I haven’t been able to find any evidence that this is deliberate (I know, for example, that the closely related feature Siri Recap can and will listen to people further away, since Apple gives the example of a lecturer “in an otherwise quiet room” in its notes) but suspect that it may relate to privacy. If the waiter leans in and tells you about today’s delicious cod cheeks, one may assume they consent to being heard. If the speaker is three tables away, things become murkier.

Live Rewind doesn’t approve of swearing

I don’t want to shock you, but while testing this feature I happened to hear a YouTuber use the word “shit.” Live Rewind transcribed this as ****. (Siri Recap did the same, incidentally.)

The closest I can find to an explanation is in the support document, where Apple says Siri Recap is “designed to omit potentially harmful content, such as language that promotes self-harm or hateful speech.” But that’s a different issue, and “shit” does not, as far as I can see, constitute hateful speech.

So it’s a bit of a mystery. But very much the sort of family-values prudishness we’ve come to expect from Apple.

David Price / Foundry

The range of privacy measures is admirable…

For better and worse, the issue of privacy is absolutely central to Live Rewind.

Apple is conscious that most of us are creeped out by the idea of a wrist-mounted surveillance bot listening in on conversations. It’s conscious that previous surveillance-adjacent tech (Google Glass, for example) has encountered significant public pushback, and wants to avoid bad PR. So everything has been done with privacy in mind.

To trigger Live Rewind, you have to double-press the Digital Crown, a distinctive gesture intended to be hard for creeps to disguise. A similar intent lies behind the on-screen animation and non-mutable sound effect, both of which alert anyone close enough to be recorded by the feature that you are summoning a transcript of what they just said.

It’s also worth mentioning that the feature works on your device. (The processing legwork happens on the companion iPhone, not the Apple Watch, by the way, so make sure it’s nearby.) It doesn’t happen in the cloud, and Apple insists it does not have access to the data.

I won’t pretend I’m completely on board with listening tech in general. I fear that such technologies are becoming more and more widespread and normalised. But with Live Rewind, Apple has done everything it can to take privacy concerns into consideration.

…and sometimes frustrating

I applaud Apple for its efforts to safeguard privacy. But like the AirTag, which quite rightly took steps to combat stalking and in the process made itself a far less effective anti-theft device, Live Rewind finds itself in a position where good intentions lead to many of its most frustrating limitations.

The short memory is there to limit the feature’s surveillance capabilities. Ditto, I suspect, the short physical range. It also doesn’t attempt, by design and for explicitly privacy-related reasons, to identify or differentiate between multiple speakers (not even “speaker A” and “speaker B”), despite this being an obvious way to make transcripts easier to parse.

When viewing the transcript on your Apple Watch, you’ll find that the screenshot function is disabled, presumably to make it slightly less convenient for bad actors to eavesdrop and then share the results. But this also makes life less convenient if you want to share them for innocent reasons, such as sending the list of specials to a latecomer on their way to the restaurant, or publishing an article about how well the feature works.

Live Rewind would be much more useful if these limitations were cast aside, but it would also be more controversial, and Apple doesn’t like that.

Mahmoud Itani / Foundry

Conclusions

I’m way more impressed by Live Rewind than I expected to be.

The accuracy is very solid. Yes, it makes some mistakes when tested under the most challenging conditions, but a lot of those mistakes will actually be phonetic best guesses that can be deciphered with little effort. And it usually gets the important details right.

It’s not quite sharp enough that you can ignore the waiter listing off specials or the senior colleague asking you a question and assume everything will be transcribed perfectly. But it’s a handy backup for the parts you missed while mostly paying attention.

The main issues I have with Live Rewind, if they can be called issues, are the limitations deliberately put in place for privacy reasons. It’s got very short range, for instance, and the 15-second memory window is on the low side in terms of usefulness. But privacy matters, and I understand why Apple made these decisions.

Speaking only for myself, I still find the concept a tiny bit creepy. But Apple has done its best to minimise that factor, and this is overall a very decent effort.

With the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display, Apple returned the Apple logo to its former glory, switching from shiny aluminum to one that lights up and glows again. Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t just the best display ever put in a laptop. It’s also Apple’s first-ever touchscreen in a Mac and the first time macOS has supported Touch as an input option. It’s a feature we longtime Mac users thought we’d never see, mostly because Apple has a history of saying it won’t happen.

But it has happened—and on the expensive laptop Apple sells, no less. While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has plenty of other features to attract customers, which I will outline in my upcoming review, the touchscreen is one of the most interesting features to come to the Mac in years and is sure to be a major consideration for buyers when choosing which laptop to get.

However, macOS with Touch isn’t the same interface that you can just reach out to control with your fingers. Apple has enhanced and optimized macOS to accommodate Touch, making the overall experience satisfying. Here are my observations after spending a few days with it.

No lag or delay

Apple did not simply take a Touch input sensor, slap it on top of the OLED, pack it all up, and ship it. For the optimal experience, the Touch sensor is incorporated into the OLED panel, just as it is with the iPad Pro. That makes it perform more like a tablet than a usual touchscreen laptop.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

It also means there’s no lag when touching the screen. Tap the screen, and you’ll get an instant reaction from macOS: buttons, menus, sliders, icons, the Dock, you name it. Everything reacts the instant you touch it.

UI clarity

My major concern about the touchscreen MacBook Pro was whether Apple would do enough (or anything) to adjust macOS’s longstanding UI elements for Touch input. Some elements in macOS need to be larger to make them easier to touch; others need to be shifted to create more space; and still others need a complete rethink. A touch UI that demands cursor-style precision means you have to concentrate to do the most mundane of tasks. That’s tiring.

Foundry

In macOS 27.2 on the new MacBook Pro, Apple has enhanced macOS to accommodate Touch. Throughout the OS, elements appear when using Touch and return to the normal view when using a mouse or trackpad. The first thing you’ll notice is the set of traffic lights that appear in the upper right corner of windows to close, minimize, or expand windows full-screen, respectively. When tapped, the red, yellow, and green buttons magnify to make the target easier to hit.

Even menu items adjust by expanding a bit to add space between the items so they’re easier to tap with your finger. Another example is checkboxes, which let you tap on the accompanying text to select as well as the box itself.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

UI confusion

Almost all of the time, I can navigate through macOS just by using Touch. Apple thoughtfully considered the elements that I encountered to make them easy to touch, with one exception: video files. The ability to watch a tiny version of the video by clicking on the “Play” icon in the center of the video’s icon gets in the way of opening the file. Double-tapping to open the video file often resulted in the video playing in the icon, not actually opening the file. It’s one of the things that hasn’t been adjusted to accommodate Touch, and it needs a retool.

I also found that the mindset for Touch on macOS is separate from iOS. My experience with Apple’s touch-based UI is mostly with iOS, so I thought that macOS Touch would work similarly. But Apple decided to stick to macOS conventions, as illustrated by opening an app. In iOS, opening an app is a single tap. In macOS, a single tap selects the app, just as a single click does with a mouse or trackpad. You need to double-tap to launch the app.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Gesture support

Multi-Touch gestures on the Mac support the same gestures that are on the trackpad and, for the most part, your iPhone and iPad. It’s all smart and effortless, especially if you already use these gestures on a trackpad: Swipe with two fingers to scroll up, down, left, or right.  Use three fingers and swipe left or right to switch desktops. A four-finger swipe up opens Mission Control. A four-finger swipe down opens App Exposé, etc.

Pinch-to-zoom even works. Rotate, where you use two fingers in a rotating motion, also works, but this gesture was awkward for me to do on a standing screen. I think it’s easier to do on a trackpad or, say, an iPad that’s lying flat.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Screen wobble

Apple re-engineered the MacBook Pro’s hinge to make the screen more stable while touching it. The hinge provides enough resistance when you’re pressing relatively softly against the screen. Push hard enough, and the screen falls back, but most of the time, you’re not going to need to push that hard. In the animation above, you can see the screen wobble as I do the rotation gesture, but it’s exaggerated since I repeated the gesture several times and inadvertently pressed harder than usual.

If you tap lightly, you won’t see the display move, but most people will tap hard enough to see a wobble. However, my regular taps caused the display to shake slightly, which was noticeable but bearable. The wobble is significantly less than a regular MacBook Pro, however, and after the first few taps, I barely noticed it.

Fingerprints

It’s a consequence of using any touchscreen: the display will end up with fingerprints smeared all over it. Like an iPad, they’re not noticeable when the display is on, but when the display goes dark or turns off, ugh. It’s gross.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

This is just a fact about touchscreens we have to live with. Even with Apple’s oleophobic coating, there just isn’t a practical way to prevent fingerprints from appearing at all. There are personal habits that can be practiced to minimize the mess: clean your hands before using the touchscreen, wipe your hands frequently, don’t eat while using a touchscreen, etc. Or you could use touch-friendly gloves, or even wear latex gloves (I tried it and it works), but that’s not practical (and it’s ridiculous). Have a microfiber cloth handy to clean the display; Apple unfortunately doesn’t include one unless you spring for the nano-texture coating, but they sell one for $9. Amazon sells a six-pack of Koala Lens Cleaning Cloths for $10.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s Touch works only with fingers, not with an Apple Pencil or any third-party stylus. Other than fingerprints, using your fingers doesn’t offer nearly the same precision as using a stylus, so it’s closer to using an iPhone rather than an iPad or a graphics tablet.

A very good start

Apple isn’t marketing the MacBook Pro as a Touch-first device. Rather, Touch is something users can turn to when the situation calls for it. But it’s promising nonetheless. This first version of the Mac’s Touch UI is smooth, reliable, usable, and even fun. It’s a good start, and I hope Apple invents ways to take advantage of Touch, evolving it beyond being a touch interface on top of macOS.

After years of rumors and speculation, Apple has finally begin shipping its first MacBook with a touchscreen. But while this may sound like a dream come true for some users, others are still trying to figure out whether this change actually makes sense. After all, the move appears to contradict principles laid down in 2010 by no less a commentator than Steve Jobs.

I’m not entirely against the idea of touchscreen Macs. There are a lot of touchscreen Windows laptops out there, and plenty of use cases to suit them. It’s just that Apple’s implementation doesn’t seem particularly effective. The touchscreen doesn’t seem to add anything new to the user experience, or to the rest of the market. In fact, the more I look at the new MacBook Pro and its marquee feature, the more I find myself missing something else: the Touch Bar.

The Touch Bar was misunderstood

The Touch Bar was an OLED strip that sat above the keyboard on MacBooks. Introduced in 2016, it replaced the classic function keys with virtual buttons that changed depending on what was on the screen; each app had its own controls. The idea seemed too good to be true when it was announced, and I was really excited about it.

Apple itself seemed to lose interest in the Touch Bar after a while and stopped adding new features. Not only that, but the Touch Bar never made its way to any Mac other than the MacBook Pro: not the MacBook Air, or Apple’s wireless keyboard for its desktops. The reality is that users didn’t have many reasons to like or prefer the Touch Bar over conventional function keys. At least physical function keys were easier to hit without looking. Perhaps it was for this reason that Apple brought back the physical Esc key on later MacBook Pro models, before finally getting rid of the Touch Bar for good.

But the Touch Bar also had its good side, like being able to adjust the MacBook’s brightness or volume with just a swipe. It was also handy to have quick controls for picking emojis or scrolling through the Final Cut Pro editing timeline. None of these features were really a must-have, but they made the Mac experience a little bit nicer. And crucially, they were accessible in a place that was easy to reach.

By contrast, Apple’s examples of how owners should use the new MacBook Pro’s touchscreen seem awkward and uncomfortable. When you use a conventional laptop, your hands sit on the keyboard and the palm rest most of the time. You don’t have to lift your arm to move the cursor and click buttons. Constantly lifting your arm to touch a screen facing you vertically seems unergonomic and tiring.

Apple

How does a touchscreen help the Mac?

One of the things that bothers me most about the new MacBook Pro is that Apple seems to be trying too hard to convince us that touching a laptop screen is something we’ve been missing. Apple showed some examples of how people can use the new touchscreen, like playing a virtual piano. I’m sure this is a fun way to show off what the new hardware can do, but in reality the average user is unlikely to do this often, if ever.

There’s a reason why the iPad works so well as a touchscreen device. You can hold it in your hands, place it flat on a table, or adjust the screen angle depending on what you’re doing. A MacBook, on the other hand, is still designed primarily around a keyboard and trackpad. There are laptops designed for touch, with screens that can be tilted at steeper angles or even flipped over so you can use them like a tablet. That’s not the case with the new MacBook Pro.

Apple is rarely the first to introduce new technologies, but it usually takes its time to get them right. We saw this with the iPhone Duo: it isn’t the first foldable phone, but it solved problems that stumped rival companies. That’s not the case with the touchscreen on the MacBook Pro. It feels like Apple added the feature just for the sake of it. The new MacBook Pro is essentially the same laptop with the same user experience, but now you can touch the screen.

Apple

Ahead of its time

That brings me back to the Touch Bar. It wasn’t perfect, but it was an idea that made more sense than the current implementation of a touchscreen on a MacBook. We had something to touch that was right at our fingertips. Perhaps it would have been successful if more apps had supported it, or if Apple had figured out how to combine it with traditional function keys for those who need them.

It’s hard to argue in favor of the Touch Bar when Apple killed it because most users weren’t interested. Still, to me it seems like a good idea that was poorly executed, or something that was ahead of its time. It was nice to see Apple trying to bring touch to the Mac in a unique way that only Apple could do.

When we heard rumors about touchscreens finally coming to the Mac, I hoped for a thoughtful execution of a long-requested feature. I wanted Apple to do more than just let users touch the screens of the MacBooks we already had. But based on the latest MacBook Pro, I have to say I’m a little disappointed.

The Touch Bar was an OLED strip that sat above the keyboard on MacBooks. Introduced in 2016, it replaced the classic function keys with virtual buttons that changed depending on what was on the screen; each app had its own controls. The idea seemed too good to be true when it was announced, and I was really excited about it.

Apple itself seemed to lose interest in the Touch Bar after a while and stopped adding new features. Not only that, but the Touch Bar never made its way to any Mac other than the MacBook Pro: not the MacBook Air, or Apple’s wireless keyboard for its desktops. The reality is that users didn’t have many reasons to like or prefer the Touch Bar over conventional function keys. At least physical function keys were easier to hit without looking. Perhaps it was for this reason that Apple brought back the physical Esc key on later MacBook Pro models, before finally getting rid of the Touch Bar for good.

But the Touch Bar also had its good side, like being able to adjust the MacBook’s brightness or volume with just a swipe. It was also handy to have quick controls for picking emojis or scrolling through the Final Cut Pro editing timeline. None of these features were really a must-have, but they made the Mac experience a little bit nicer. And crucially, they were accessible in a place that was easy to reach.

By contrast, Apple’s examples of how owners should use the new MacBook Pro’s touchscreen seem awkward and uncomfortable. When you use a conventional laptop, your hands sit on the keyboard and the palm rest most of the time. You don’t have to lift your arm to move the cursor and click buttons. Constantly lifting your arm to touch a screen facing you vertically seems unergonomic and tiring.

Apple

How does a touchscreen help the Mac?

One of the things that bothers me most about the new MacBook Pro is that Apple seems to be trying too hard to convince us that touching a laptop screen is something we’ve been missing. Apple showed some examples of how people can use the new touchscreen, like playing a virtual piano. I’m sure this is a fun way to show off what the new hardware can do, but in reality the average user is unlikely to do this often, if ever.

There’s a reason why the iPad works so well as a touchscreen device. You can hold it in your hands, place it flat on a table, or adjust the screen angle depending on what you’re doing. A MacBook, on the other hand, is still designed primarily around a keyboard and trackpad. There are laptops designed for touch, with screens that can be tilted at steeper angles or even flipped over so you can use them like a tablet. That’s not the case with the new MacBook Pro.

Apple is rarely the first to introduce new technologies, but it usually takes its time to get them right. We saw this with the iPhone Duo: it isn’t the first foldable phone, but it solved problems that stumped rival companies. That’s not the case with the touchscreen on the MacBook Pro. It feels like Apple added the feature just for the sake of it. The new MacBook Pro is essentially the same laptop with the same user experience, but now you can touch the screen.

Apple

Ahead of its time

That brings me back to the Touch Bar. It wasn’t perfect, but it was an idea that made more sense than the current implementation of a touchscreen on a MacBook. We had something to touch that was right at our fingertips. Perhaps it would have been successful if more apps had supported it, or if Apple had figured out how to combine it with traditional function keys for those who need them.

It’s hard to argue in favor of the Touch Bar when Apple killed it because most users weren’t interested. Still, to me it seems like a good idea that was poorly executed, or something that was ahead of its time. It was nice to see Apple trying to bring touch to the Mac in a unique way that only Apple could do.

When we heard rumors about touchscreens finally coming to the Mac, I hoped for a thoughtful execution of a long-requested feature. I wanted Apple to do more than just let users touch the screens of the MacBooks we already had. But based on the latest MacBook Pro, I have to say I’m a little disappointed.

  • M5 Pro and M5 Max

Apple made no indication that there was any CPU/GPU performance increase over an equivalent non-touch M5 configuration, or a quantified improvement in whole-system power efficiency.

Separately, Apple has launched the 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip.

There is no increase in base or maximum memory over the equivalent non-touch M5 models. The M5 Pro starts with 24GB, the 32-core GPU M5 Max has 36GB, and the 40-core version starts with 48GB.

Reaching 64GB with M5 Pro requires the 20-core GPU; reaching 128GB requires the 40-core M5 Max.

More memory can accommodate larger creative projects, more demanding multitasking and larger local AI models.

Touchscreen MacBook storage: What is the highest capacity?

The entry capacities are unchanged. However, it is possible to upgrade to 16TB on M5 Max, up from 8TB. In order to obtain that capacity buyers need either the 32-core or 40-core GPU.

The camera remains a 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View and 1080p video recording. Advanced video stabilisation is new, however.

Authentication remains Touch ID. Dynamic Island is an interface feature, not confirmation of Face ID or a TrueDepth camera.

Apple retains a six-speaker system, force-cancelling woofers, Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support. Apple claims 50% deeper bass and adds closed-lid audio tuning.

The three-microphone array retains directional beamforming, Voice Isolation and Wide Spectrum modes.

Touchscreen MacBook battery

Apple lists video-streaming ratings of 22/20 hours for the 14-inch Pro/Max and 24/22 hours for the 16-inch Pro/Max, the same as the non-touchscreen models.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro connectivity and ports

Both sizes include:

  • One 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones.
  • Three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C ports, supporting charging and DisplayPort.
  • One HDMI port.
  • One SDXC card slot.
  • MagSafe 3.

Apple quotes Thunderbolt/USB4 support up to 120Gb/s and DisplayPort 2.1.

Apple’s N1 wireless chip, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread are included, but they are not touchscreen-model upgrades.

External display support

The M5 Pro chip supports three external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz. Alternatively, it can support one 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz display, plus a second at up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz.

The M5 Max chip supports four external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or two displays at up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz.

Apple’s PROLED XDR specifications lists 165Hz for the multi-display 4K configurations, rather than the older 144Hz figure.
